title: Two weaknesses: add a second target
outcomes: Finds the weak pawns (isolated or backward) of a side and the one you already attack
Finds a move that attacks a second weak pawn while the first stays attacked
Does not play the second-target move when the engine rates it clearly worse
Says when there is no weak pawn to attack

steps.text: One weak pawn can usually be defended by tying a piece to it. A second weakness stretches the defence: his pieces cannot guard both. When you already attack one weak pawn, look for a move that attacks a second **without letting go of the first**. *Rule of thumb:* two targets need two ways of attacking them. Single targets: "Weak pawns: targets only if you can attack them".

steps.caption: Black to move. White has two weak pawns, on a2 and c4 (both isolated). Black already attacks a2 with the rook on a6.

line.say: The rook moves to b4 and now attacks c4 too, while a2 stays attacked.

claims.statement: White's pawn on a2 is isolated.
White's pawn on c4 is isolated.
No Black piece attacks c4 now.
After Rb4, 1 Black piece(s) attack a2.
After Rb4, 1 Black piece(s) attack c4.
After Rb4, no White piece attacks the rook.
At depth 16 Rb4 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: Creating weaknesses is not progress in itself. A second target helps only if you can really attack it and the pressure on the first goes on. It fails when the extra move costs you more elsewhere, and it does not apply when no weak pawn exists. Compare the three positions below.

steps.title: A second target, too costly, nothing to attack
steps.prompt: Predict which statement fits each position. In the second, a White knight has moved from f3 to b3; the third is a different position. Then name the one change that flipped the verdict between the first two.

Paper exercise (the app does not check it): take a game where you attacked one weak pawn and the opponent defended it. Write which second weakness you could have created and which of your pieces would attack it.
